doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: New synthesizer project with Pat Gleason
summary: He is working with synthesist Patrick Gleeson on a piano concerto with synthesized orchestra, and discusses modern studios.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Um hum. There actually was a whole decade that I was immersed in a kind of a multiple keyboard integration of classical, rock, jazz, funk and electronic music. It started in the late 60s, around ’67, ’68. Well before there were any kind of polyphonic synthesizers around or even portable monophonic ones. It was maybe just as the ARP 2600 was coming out. Mainly it was Moog synthesizers with patch cords and stuff. And I got engineers to build me modules and things and ring modulators. And I gradually put together a rig that looked like a 747 cockpit. Six different keyboard instruments in stacks at right angles to each other, miles of cords and foot switches and foot pedals. It took six hours to tear this thing down from my studio, load it onto a truck, take it to a gig, play the gig and then six hours to undo it. But I loved it. For about ten years this was the way I performed and recorded. I did several albums of this kind of stuff. And it actually was at the time of my leave taking with Columbia Records. They didn’t want to embark on this particular journey with me and I can’t blame them. It didn’t have much commercial potential at all. So I put out the first album myself on Double Helix Records. And so for about ten years I was doing a lot of that kind of work, and that period really culminated with this “Invasion of the Body Snatchers” score in ’78. So it was about a ten year period. And when that was over I’d not only had had enough of movie scores, I had a hunger for the purity of acoustic music. And for many years I did almost no electronics at all, just acoustic piano in various contexts. And it’s only in this last year that I’m currently involved in a very interesting project with a synthesist and a recording studio guy named Pat Gleason, very talented guy. He was, you may remember he was the first synthesist to go on the road with a jazz group.

Right. And so Patrick and I have known each other for a long time. In the 60s he was the guy who first told me to take this cord and plug it here when I wanted to learn what a Moog synthesizer was about. So we’re doing a project together, just totally on spec which is kind of a piano concerto orchestral format where the orchestra is synthesized. And we’re having a ball. It’s my first big foray back into electronics in many years.
Yeah. The toys have changed a lot.

Oh yeah, the toys changed. It’s just amazing what’s out there now. And I’m very glad to have someone who is immersed in it as thoroughly as Pat is, because it would be very hard now to do all the music and all the electronics and all the recording yourself. I mean God—
You think back what a Prophet cost when it was in its heyday. For the same amount of money now you could get an awful lot.
You can indeed and yet it still ends up people like Pat who have studios like this, it’s a multi-million dollar expense when they really get into it. Because he’s got every sample

library known to man, and every kind of hardware bus and all the software and microphones. It’s endless. And it’s a full time commitment to know how to use a studio like that. He’s constantly reading the updated manual for this latest software that’s got five hundred pages of these — so it’s a huge commitment these days to be up on that stuff. So to me it makes sense to collaborate with someone like that. He brings that to the table, I bring the composition and the performing to the table. And I think something very interesting is happening.
